query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys exposed above 900 °C, the identity of the minor element X (Si, Mn, or Al) governs the formation and persistence of a stable, coherent protective oxide layer by controlling the nature and growth kinetics of the oxide scale. Specifically, when X is Si or Al the alloy forms a slow‐growing, adherent oxide (e.g., a SiO2‐ or Al2O3‐rich layer, potentially supported by Cr2O3) that minimizes oxygen and cation diffusion and reduces thermal mismatch stresses, whereas when X is Mn the resulting oxide mix is more prone to developing unstable, cracking/spalling surface scales.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX alloys synthesized as single- or multiphase metallic solid solutions.
generation.intervention: Vary the alloying element X among Si, Mn, and Al while keeping other processing parameters constant.
generation.conditions: Exposure at temperatures above 900 °C in an oxidative and/or corrosive atmosphere.
generation.structural_mediator: The composition, thickness, and coherence of the surface oxide scale; in particular, the formation of a continuous SiO2 or Al2O3 (and associated Cr2O3) layer versus a discontinuous oxide mix featuring Mn-oxides.
generation.mechanism: Si or Al additives favor the formation of a protective, low-growth-rate oxide due to their thermodynamic stability and lower diffusivity in the oxide, which leads to a well-adhered and coherent scale. In contrast, Mn promotes the formation of oxides that lack these protective qualities, due to higher diffusivity and greater thermal expansion mismatch, leading to stress accumulation and eventual cracking or spallation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical high-temperature oxidative conditions, alloys with Si or Al will develop a stable, coherent oxide layer that persists over time (showing low spallation and minimal surface degradation) compared to the baseline alloy with Mn, which will exhibit unstable oxides that crack or spall.
generation.baseline: CrFeCoNiMn alloy, under the same processing and exposure conditions.
generation.boundary: The mechanism applies to alloys in a metallic solid-solution state (either single- or multiphase) exposed above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres typical of practical high-temperature service environments.
generation.uncertainty: While the general trends are supported by known effects of Si and Al in promoting protective oxides in other alloy systems, the specific kinetics, scale thicknesses, and exact diffusion barriers in these CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys remain to be quantified. The interplay with the multi-principal element matrix may also introduce additional complexities that require further study.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three sets of CrFeCoNiX alloy samples with X = Si, Mn, or Al using identical processing routes to ensure a similar single- or multiphase solid solution. Expose all samples to a controlled oxidative atmosphere (e.g., air with controlled moisture) at temperatures >900 °C for a defined time. Characterize the oxide scale by scanning electron microscopy (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and adhesion tests (e.g., scratch or pull-off testing) to assess continuity, thickness, and mechanical integrity.
measurements: Oxide scale composition (using energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy, EDS)
Oxide scale morphology and continuity (SEM/TEM imaging)
Adhesion quality (mechanical testing such as pull-off or scratch tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloys with X = Si or Al do not show a statistically significant improvement in oxide scale coherence, adhesion, and resistance to spallation relative to the Mn-containing alloy under these conditions, or if the Mn-alloy unexpectedly exhibits a stable, coherent oxide layer comparable to or exceeding that of the Si/Al alloys, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Enhanced properties are one of the key motivations for research on high entropy alloys (HEA) and compositionally complex alloys (CCA) []. Miracle and Senkov [] stated that “HEAs have been tightly associated with finding single-phase solid solutions by controlling configurational entropy”. Furthermore, and in line with a proposal by Miracle and Senkov [], we refer to multi-principal element alloys forming multiphase microstructures as complex concentrated alloys (CCAs). Contrary to the conventional alloys, HEAs are defined to contain five to 13 major constituting elements where the concentration of each element ranges from 5 to 35 at.% []. According to Zhang et al., the formation of HEAs is predicted for materials exhibiting 12 J K−1∙mol−1 (≈ 1.44∙R) ≤ configurational entropies ≤ 17.5 J∙K−1 mol−1 (≈ 2.10 R), −10 kJ∙mol−1 ≤ enthalpies of mixing ≤ 5 kJ∙mol−1 and atomic size differences ≤ 5% [], with R as the gas constant (≈ 8.3144 J K−1∙mol−1). However, over time, these guidelines were revealed not to be entirely successful at predicting the formation of single-phase solid solutions [,,,,].

The alloys JZ3 and JZ3+ could be considered to be RCCAs [], see Section 2.2.2. The density of both alloys was lower than the upper density value of (a) transition metal HEA (9 g/cm3 []), (b) single phase bcc solid solution RCCAs with Al, Nb and Ta additions (9.08 g/cm3 []) and (c) multiphase bcc solid solution + intermetallic(s) (Laves, M5Si3) RCCAs with Al, Nb and Ta or Cr, Nb and Ta additions (8.58 g/cm3 []).
